newsitem.title: USA: Health of China's banks debated after DRI report.
newsitem.headline: Health of China's banks debated after DRI report.

text.p: U.S. economic forecast firm DRI/McGraw Hill sparked heated discussions in financial markets when it said on Tuesday that China's troubled banking sector represented "one of the most serious threats" to global market stability.

"Although reforms of the Chinese banking industry may contain the problem over the short-term, the risk of a serious debt problem will continue to mount and could have major economic ramifications for many of China's smaller and weaker economic neighbors," the report said.

Views of the DRI/McGraw Hill report among U.S. analysts ranged from complimentary to harshly critical. Criticism focused particularly on the contention that China's banks had an "enormous" problem with non-performing loans.

In the report, DRI/McGraw Hill chief international economist Nariman Behravesh said that within the next three to five years, China could see defaults on between 20 and 40 percent of the country's $600 billion in outstanding loans.
"It's absolutely false and incredibly misleading," said Robert Visek, vice president at Chase Manhattan Bank.
"This is still one of the fastest growing economies in the world. China will outgrow its problems," Visek said.

Behravesh said Chinese banks have been crippled by government policies that forced them to make questionable loans to state-owned or state-sponsored companies, many of which were in weak financial positions.

"The banking sector is in extreme crisis. It's a gigantic problem, the banks are essentially owned by the public sector," one U.S.-based emerging market analyst said. "It's something that would have extreme reprecussions for both China and now Hong Kong."

U.S. analysts concurred that most Chinese banks have enormous loans outstanding to domestic state firms, which may not be able to repay. But they differed in interpreting the implications of these non-paying loans.

Chase's Visek said banking problems had nothing to do with the risk of a foreign investor doing business in the country. He added that foreign banks doing business in China were increasing their loan portfolios 40 to 50 percent per year.
He said there was nothing wrong with the banks keeping the companies afloat because interest was being paid, and the banks would not go bankrupt.

"If the banks don't go bankrupt and the government does not go bankrupt, then what is the negative for the world economy?" Visek said, adding that the state-owned sector was shrinking as a proportion of the overall economy.
